Anchored between Lake Pontchartrain and one of the most remarkable cities in the world is a university with strong academic programs, real careers, and people who show up for each other. LSU New Orleans is where Privateers make their mark.

Counselor Education Doctoral Program Receives Outstanding Program Award
LSU New Orleans' Counselor Education Doctoral Program has received the 2026 Outstanding Doctoral Counselor Education and Supervision Program Award from the Southern Association for Counselor Education and Supervision (SACES).
The award recognizes the program's contributions to counselor education, including its commitment to research, leadership and preparing future counselor educators. The program was honored during the SACES 2026 Conference in Louisville, Kentucky, on Nov. 6.
LSU New Orleans is home to the only CACREP-accredited Counselor Education doctoral program at a public institution in Louisiana. Over the past five years, 70% of its doctoral graduates completed the program with at least one peer-reviewed publication, research grant or award from a national or state counseling organization. Half of those graduates earned accomplishments in at least two of those categories.
The program's impact extends well beyond campus. Approximately 70% of its graduates from the past decade work in higher education. Alumni currently serve as faculty in 12 of Louisiana's 15 counselor education programs and in more than 30 graduate programs nationwide.
Faculty members Anabel Mifsud and Chris Belser participated in the recognition, which highlights the program's continued contributions to counselor education and the development of future leaders in the profession.

LSU New Orleans Receives Grant to Support City of Covington’s Flood Preparedness Efforts
LSU New Orleans’ Center for Hazards Assessment, Response and Technology (CHART) has received a $10,311 award to support the City of Covington, Louisiana, in preparing for an upcoming verification visit through the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Community Rating System (CRS).
Led by Principal Investigator Monica Teets Farris, the project will provide technical assistance to the city ahead of its scheduled CRS verification visit in November. The effort will focus on reviewing, organizing and documenting activities that may qualify for credit under the CRS program.
The CRS is a voluntary FEMA program that recognizes communities taking steps to reduce flood risk and improve floodplain management. Participating communities can earn credit for activities that go beyond minimum floodplain management requirements, potentially helping residents qualify for discounts on flood insurance premiums.
As part of the project, CHART will work with the City of Covington to review eligible CRS activities that fall into four categories: public information, mapping and regulations, flood damage reduction and warning and response.
CHART will help the city assess its existing efforts and document activities that demonstrate its commitment to flood risk reduction and community preparedness.
The project reflects LSU New Orleans’ commitment to applying its expertise to real-world challenges facing Louisiana communities. Through its work with Covington, CHART will support local efforts to strengthen flood preparedness, improve documentation of mitigation activities and promote community resilience.

Privateer Basketball Legend Ervin Johnson Named Fall Commencement Speaker
Former NBA player and LSU New Orleans alumnus Ervin Johnson will return to the Lakefront Arena as the keynote speaker for the university's fall 2026 commencement ceremony on Friday, Dec. 11, at 10 a.m.
A New Orleans native and 13-year NBA veteran, Johnson earned his bachelor's degree from the university in 1997. He returned to his alma mater in August as assistant men's basketball coach.
“Ervin Johnson's story is nothing short of extraordinary. He overcame circumstances that could have defined or limited his future, yet through remarkable determination, discipline and perseverance, he achieved a level of success that very few people ever reach,” said Jeanette Weiland, interim chancellor and chief administrative officer of LSU New Orleans.
Johnson played for the Privateers from 1989 to 1993, helping lead the team to three conference championships and two NCAA Tournament appearances. During his senior season, the Privateers finished undefeated in Sun Belt Conference play with an 18-0 record. He was named the 1993 Sun Belt Conference Player of the Year and set 26 school records during his collegiate career.
Selected in the first round of the 1993 NBA Draft by the Seattle SuperSonics, Johnson went on to play 13 seasons with Seattle, Denver, Milwaukee and Minnesota. He appeared in 845 NBA games and was part of Seattle's 1996 NBA Finals team.
Following his NBA career, Johnson dedicated much of his time to mentoring young athletes and supporting community programs. He served as a community ambassador for the Denver Nuggets for nearly 15 years and founded Ervin Johnson Hoops, a nonprofit basketball program focused on developing young female athletes.
His accomplishments have earned him induction into the Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame, the Greater New Orleans Sports Hall of Fame and the Privateer Athletics Hall of Fame.
For Johnson, returning to campus to address graduates carries special meaning.
“Coming back to LSU New Orleans has meant so much to me because this university helped shape the person I am today,” Johnson said. “As the first person in my family to earn a college degree, I know firsthand how education can change the direction of someone's life. I look forward to sharing my experiences with our graduates and encouraging them to believe in themselves, work hard and make a difference wherever life takes them.”
The fall commencement ceremony will take place Friday, Dec. 11, at 10 a.m. at the Lakefront Arena, 6801 Franklin Ave.

A New Chapter, A Shared Tradition: Homecoming Returns Nov. 7
As LSU New Orleans prepares to celebrate its first Homecoming under its new name, the university is bringing together generations of Privateers to honor familiar traditions, create new memories, and celebrate the next chapter in its history.
This year's Homecoming festivities will feature returning favorites, new activities, and opportunities for students and alumni to reconnect with the university community.
For current students, the celebration represents an opportunity to embrace the excitement surrounding LSU New Orleans while continuing the traditions that have long defined the Privateer experience.
“Homecoming is always such a wonderful time of celebration and reflection on what it means to be a Privateer!” said Joy Ballard, Director of Student Involvement and Leadership. “I hope our current students see this new era as an opportunity to continue honoring all the things that make being a Privateer so great, but with a little extra energy and excitement.”
Several familiar traditions will return, including the annual tailgate, Homecoming Royalty elections, and the student organization competition for the Homecoming Spirit Award. Popular activities such as the petting zoo and silent disco will also be back.
This year will introduce new opportunities for students to participate, including a Tailgate Favorites Cookoff and invitations for students from select affinity groups to attend the Alumni Privateer Social.
Ballard said she is especially excited to see student organizations compete for the first LSU New Orleans Homecoming Spirit Award and to crown the university's first Homecoming Royalty in purple and gold.
While students look forward to making new memories, Homecoming also offers alumni an opportunity to reconnect with the university that helped shape their lives.
For Natalie Beck, LSU New Orleans' new Director of Alumni Engagement, the celebration carries special meaning. An alumna herself, Beck earned her first two degrees from the university in 2005 and her master's degree in 2007. Now, she returns to campus professionally as the university begins a new chapter.
“Welcoming alumni home under a new name means telling them that those experiences still count,” Beck said. “This Homecoming is a chance to say that every graduate, no matter which name was on the sign, is part of one family.”
Beck emphasized that although the university's name has changed, the experiences, relationships, and traditions shared by generations of graduates remain part of its identity.
“You are not just being welcomed to something new. You are being welcomed back to something that grew because of you,” she said.
She also hopes Homecoming will strengthen connections between alumni and current students, creating opportunities to exchange experiences, advice and ideas.
“Alumni have wisdom about careers, resilience, and finding your path. Students have energy, fresh ideas, and a view of where the university is headed,” Beck said.
For Ballard, the significance of this year's celebration extends beyond the events themselves.
“I hope they remember the energy and excitement of this time in our university’s history,” Ballard said. “I hope they remember being part of something new and feeling genuinely excited to be a Privateer!”
Cheria Scaffidi, Executive Director of University Advancement and President of the LSU New Orleans Foundation, said Homecoming represents an opportunity to celebrate the university's legacy while looking ahead to its future.
“There’s a new energy on the Lakefront, and you can feel it! Homecoming brings generations of Privateers together to celebrate the legacy we’ve built and the exciting future we’re creating at LSU New Orleans. And our alumni are the heartbeat of both!”
As LSU New Orleans celebrates its first Homecoming under its new name, the occasion serves as a reminder that while the university continues to evolve, the traditions, memories, and connections that define the Privateer community remain.

Four Finalists Named in Search for LSU New Orleans Chancellor
Four finalists have been selected in the search for LSU New Orleans' next chancellor, LSU System President Wade Rousse announced. The candidates will visit campus Nov. 3 and 4 to meet with faculty, staff, students and community members.
“LSU New Orleans has tremendous potential, and selecting the right leader is critical to realizing that potential,” Rousse said. “These four finalists bring a wide range of experience and proven leadership in higher education. I'm confident that our next chancellor will help us build on the university's strengths, expand opportunities for students and position LSU New Orleans for long-term success.”
The four finalists bring experience in university leadership, academic affairs, student success and institutional growth.
Meet the Finalists
Sebastian van Delden, Ph.D.
Van Delden currently serves as provost and vice president for academic affairs at Winthrop University. He previously held leadership positions at the College of Charleston, Southeastern Louisiana University and USC Upstate. His background includes research in artificial intelligence and robotics, academic program development and securing funding for STEM initiatives. He earned his doctorate in computer science from the University of Central Florida.
Michael J. Savoie, Ph.D.
Savoie is vice provost at the University of North Texas at Frisco and dean of its College of Applied and Collaborative Studies. He previously held leadership positions at Southern Methodist University, Utah Valley University and UT Dallas. His work focuses on technology, organizational improvement and higher education leadership. An LSU graduate, Savoie also holds an MBA from Nicholls State University and a doctorate from the University of North Texas.
Jeanette R. Weiland
Weiland currently serves as interim chancellor and chief administrative officer of LSU New Orleans, leading the university through its transition into the LSU System. She has more than 20 years of leadership experience in higher education, healthcare and economic development, including previous roles at Tulane University, the New Orleans Business Alliance and Ochsner Health. She earned her bachelor's degree from LSU and two master's degrees from the University of New Orleans.
Kent L. Willis, Ph.D.
Willis serves as senior vice president for enrollment and student engagement at Stephen F. Austin State University, where his leadership contributed to record freshman enrollment and a 7% increase in overall enrollment. He previously held leadership positions at California State University, Fresno, and within the University of Texas System. His experience includes student success, enrollment management and university administration. He earned his doctorate in educational management from Hampton University and is a UC Berkeley Executive Leadership Academy fellow.
Next Steps
The finalists will participate in campus visits Nov. 3 and 4, providing opportunities for the university community to learn more about each candidate and their vision for LSU New Orleans.
The chancellor search comes as LSU New Orleans continues its transition into the LSU System, with an emphasis on academic excellence, financial sustainability and expanding opportunities for students.

Computer Science Professor Dr. Abdullah Al Redwan Newaz Awarded NSF and LBRN Funding for Robotics Research
Dr. Abdullah Al Redwan Newaz, assistant professor in the Department of Computer Science at LSU New Orleans and director of the Autonomous Intelligent Robotics (AiR) Lab, has been awarded funding for two research projects that use robotics and artificial intelligence to address a shared challenge: how autonomous systems make decisions under uncertainty. The projects focus on water quality monitoring and robot-assisted therapy for children with autism spectrum disorder.
The first project, “ERI: AQUABOT: Advancing Water Quality Monitoring with an Intelligent Bot via Integrated Learning and Decision-Making,” received an award from the National Science Foundation and will run from August 2026 through April 2027.
The research focuses on improving how water quality is monitored across Louisiana’s coastal waters. Traditional monitoring relies on crews traveling by boat to collect samples at predetermined locations. While effective, the approach is costly and time-consuming and captures only a limited snapshot of conditions across large bodies of water.
Dr. Newaz’s team will develop an autonomous boat capable of determining where it should collect its next water sample based on what it has already learned. As the boat moves through the water, it will use its measurements to build a continuously updated map of water quality, identify areas where that map is least certain and navigate to those locations for additional sampling.
The key idea is to combine two tasks that are usually handled separately: learning from water-quality measurements and deciding where to measure next. Rather than following routes planned in advance, AQUABOT will adapt its route in real time based on the information it gathers.
Dr. Newaz will also receive funding for the project “Next Generation Multirobot Applied Behavior Analysis Therapy for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder” from the Louisiana Biomedical Research Network (LBRN) at LSU, which is supported by the National Institutes of Health. The project will also run from August 2026 through April 2027.
The project brings together researchers from multiple disciplines to explore how social robots can help expand access to applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy. ABA is widely used to support children with autism, but access is limited because treatment typically requires one-on-one sessions with trained therapists. The cost and scarcity of those services can create long waits for families seeking care.
Dr. Newaz and his collaborators will develop social robots designed to engage children ages 3 to 12 in interactive activities focused on skills such as turn-taking, joint attention and storytelling. The activities will incorporate core components of ABA therapy while allowing the robots to adjust difficulty in response to each child. Researchers will use standardized cognitive and behavioral assessments to measure changes over the course of the study.
The robots are not intended to replace therapists. Instead, the team envisions the technology as a way to extend the reach of clinicians, giving children additional opportunities to practice skills between appointments and in settings such as homes and schools.
Dr. Newaz is joined on the project by co-principal investigators Dr. Md Tamjidul Hoque, Dr. James Wagner, Dr. Ben Samuel and Dr. Elliott Beaton.
Together, the projects advance research at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence and real-world applications, with potential benefits for communities across Louisiana and beyond.

The numbers behind the story
72%
of undergraduate students receive grants or scholarships
An affordable education shouldn't be out of reach. At LSU New Orleans, nine out of ten incoming full-time students receive some form of financial assistance, and across all undergraduates, more than $41 million in financial aid and scholarships is awarded every year. On average, students who receive grants or scholarships get nearly $10,000 toward their education, putting a quality degree within reach.
90%
employed within two years after graduating
90% of our students are employed two years after graduation according to Niche.com. LSU New Orleans has been ranked top in the state in lowest student debt and number one in Louisiana in highest early career salaries.
1958
Founded in New Orleans
LSU New Orleans emerged as a public research institution committed to making higher education accessible to the region. The university developed strong academic programs while celebrating the city's distinctive cultural traditions, becoming a vital pathway for economic opportunity and regional prosperity.

Where is LSU New Orleans located?
LSU New Orleans sits on the scenic shores of Lake Pontchartrain at 2000 Lakeshore Drive in New Orleans, LA 70148. You can take a virtual tour from home or schedule an in-person visit to experience the campus for yourself. View the campus map for a full layout and directions.
What does tuition cost at LSU New Orleans?
LSU New Orleans is consistently ranked among the nation's most affordable universities. Tuition varies based on residency status and credit hours. For a full breakdown of current rates and an estimated cost of attendance, visit the Tuition and Fees page.
What degree programs does LSU New Orleans offer?
LSU New Orleans offers a wide range of undergraduate, graduate, and doctoral programs across multiple colleges. Whether you're exploring a specific major or just getting started, browse all programs of study to find the right fit.
How do I apply to LSU New Orleans?
Applying is straightforward: submit your application online, send official transcripts, and check your portal for your admission status. Visit the Apply page to get started.
Is on-campus housing available?
Yes. On-campus housing is available in a variety of room types, so there's likely an option that fits your needs and budget. Spots fill up quickly, so it's worth applying early. Explore housing options and apply at The Office of Residential Life.
